passage: For nearly three weeks the same eight bars of Raag Yaman came through Jyoti's door every evening, and to my ears they sounded exactly the same each time. I'm Ankita, her mother, and I'll admit I was tired of them too. One night she stopped halfway, laid the sitar across her lap and stared at the wall. Two easy sentences rose in me. 'You can drop the classes if you want.' Or: 'Finish it by Diwali and I'll buy you those new earphones.' I swallowed both. I sat on her bed and said, 'Same notes again and again. It's boring, na?' She looked up, surprised, and nodded. Then I found the clip I had recorded last March, when she could barely keep the rhythm, and played it. She groaned and covered her face. 'I sounded like that?' Ten minutes later the eight bars started again.

qa.q: What did Ankita play for Jyoti?
qa.a: Ankita played the clip she had recorded last March, when Jyoti could barely keep the rhythm.

qa.q: How can you tell Jyoti was feeling stuck and fed up before her mother spoke?
qa.a: She stopped halfway, laid the sitar across her lap and stared at the wall, which suggests she was bored and discouraged by practice that seemed to go nowhere 😔

qa.q: At this point, which choice helped Jyoti more than a reward or an offer to quit, and why?
qa.a: Naming the boredom out loud and then showing her the old recording helped, because it proved her progress was real even though she could not hear it day to day.

qa.q: How might Jyoti have felt if her mother had said she could simply drop the classes?
qa.a: She might have heard it as her mother giving up on her, or felt tempted to stop just when the hard part was quietly paying off.

grounding: It shows a parent watching a teen stuck on the same piece, resisting quitting or rewards, and instead naming the boredom and pointing back to earlier progress.

passage:
Note for Mrs Pereira, keyboard teacher, from Siddharth's father, Manoj.
Week of 12 August.
Siddharth has played the left-hand run in the second page of the Clementi sonatina every day since your last class. To me it sounds no better than on day one. On Wednesday he banged the keys, said 'This is pointless, Papa' and went to his room. I nearly told him he could stop lessons after the exam. I also caught myself about to offer him a hundred rupees for every clean run. Instead I knocked and said, 'Doing one thing for two weeks is dull. I'd be bored too.' He shrugged, but he listened. I showed him his practice diary from January, where he wrote 'can't find middle C without looking.' He smiled a little. He practised again on Thursday and Friday without being asked. I thought you should know.

qa.q: Which part of the sonatina has Siddharth been practising every day?
qa.a: He has been practising the left-hand run in the second page of the Clementi sonatina.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he banged the keys and said 'This is pointless'?
qa.a: He was frustrated and bored, and seemed to believe all his practice was getting him nowhere.

qa.q: What turning point did Manoj reach at this stage, and what did it change?
qa.a: He dropped the ideas of letting Siddharth quit or paying him, admitted the practice was dull, and showed his January diary; after that Siddharth practised again without being asked.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pereira see Siddharth's plateau after reading this note?
qa.a: The teacher may see that his stuck phase is normal and that he needs reminders of past progress, not just more pressure in class.

grounding: It shows a father watching his teen's plateau, tempted by quitting or rewards, who instead acknowledges the boredom and points to earlier progress.

passage:
Tuesday night.
Wasim has played the same first page of the sonatina for eleven days. I know every wrong note by now: the same slip in bar nine, then a thump on the keys. Tonight he said, "Ammi, what's the point? I'm not getting better."
I nearly said, "Leave it then." I also nearly promised him the new cricket bat if he kept going till Diwali. Both would have been easier than sitting with his mood.
Instead I told him, "Yes, this page is boring. Eleven days of one page would bore anyone." Then I found the video from March, when he couldn't play with both hands together at all. He watched it with his mouth open and laughed at himself.
He practised for twenty more minutes. Bar nine still slips. I'm writing this down so I remember what worked.
Afreen

qa.q: Which bar keeps going wrong when Wasim plays?
qa.a: The same slip in bar nine.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she was tempted to offer the cricket bat?
qa.a: Afreen felt tired and uneasy with Wasim's low mood; letting him quit or bribing him both looked easier than staying with his frustration.

qa.q: What turning point does the video from March offer at this stage?
qa.a: It shows Wasim real progress that daily practice had hidden, so the boredom feels like part of the path rather than proof of failure.

qa.q: What is Wasim going through on the eleventh day?
qa.a: He is bored and discouraged, hearing the same mistake every night and wondering if the effort is going anywhere.

grounding: A parent watches a teen stuck on one piece, resists offering quitting or a reward, names the boredom and points back to earlier progress.

passage:
Deepika: mum can u stop listening at my door 😤
Jasleen: I was only bringing chai! You've played that same song since Sunday.
Deepika: and it STILL sounds bad. the chord change in the chorus. every time.
Deepika: honestly I might quit. my friend learned this in a week
Jasleen: Want me to say fine, quit? Or should I bribe you with a new phone cover? 😅
Deepika: lol both??
Jasleen: Truthfully, I'd be bored stiff playing one song for five days too.
Jasleen: But in June, my girl, you cried because your fingers couldn't hold a single chord. Today I heard four clean ones before the chorus.
Deepika: ...you counted?
Jasleen: I'm your mum. I count everything.
Deepika: ok fine. 15 more mins. then chai
Jasleen: Deal ❤️

qa.q: Which part of the song keeps going wrong for Deepika?
qa.a: The chord change in the chorus.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's message about being bored stiff suggest she understands?
qa.a: She understands that Deepika is bored and discouraged rather than lazy, and she feels sympathy instead of annoyance.

qa.q: What small step at this plateau helps Deepika continue?
qa.a: Admitting the song has become boring and pointing back to June, when she couldn't hold one chord, so Deepika can see how far she has come.

qa.q: What is the plateau like for Deepika right now?
qa.a: It is frustrating and a little embarrassing; she hears the same mistake every day and compares herself with a friend who learned faster.

grounding: A mother watching her teen stall on one song jokes about quitting or a reward, then acknowledges the boredom and names earlier progress.

passage:
The power went out at seven, and on the dark verandah of their house in the kasba, Arnab kept playing the same tabla kayda he had played every evening for three weeks. Rehana, shelling peas by the lantern, could hear exactly where it broke: the fast line, always the same stumble, then a hard slap on the drum.
"Enough," he muttered. "I'm fifteen and I sound like a beginner."
Her first thought was to tell him to drop it before the Saraswati Puja programme. Her second was to promise him the bicycle. She said neither.
"Three weeks on one kayda would make anyone yawn," she said. "Last year at the mela you couldn't even keep teentaal steady. Masterji shook his head at you. Tonight you kept it through the whole slow part."
Arnab stopped. "I did?"
"Twice."
He wiped his palms on his shorts and started again, slower.

qa.q: What was Rehana doing while Arnab practised?
qa.a: She was shelling peas by the lantern.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling as she listened to the same stumble every evening?
qa.a: She was tempted to let Arnab quit or bribe him with the bicycle, but she felt for his boredom and chose patience instead.

qa.q: What turning point does Rehana use at this plateau?
qa.a: She admits the kayda is boring and reminds Arnab of last year's mela, when he couldn't keep teentaal steady, so he sees his real progress.

qa.q: What is Arnab experiencing when he says he sounds like a beginner?
qa.a: He feels frustrated and a little ashamed, because three weeks of effort seem to have gone nowhere.

grounding: A mother notices her teen's plateau on the tabla, holds back from quitting or rewards, and helps by naming the boredom and earlier progress.

passage: In their flat in Toronto, Ada listened from the kitchen as Yuki played the same page of the nocturne for the ninth evening in a row, stumbling at the same bar each time. Last week Ada had tried two things. First: "If you nail it by Sunday, we'll get pizza." Yuki rolled her eyes. Then: "You know, you don't have to keep going with piano if you hate it." Yuki went silent for an hour. Tonight Ada tried something different. She sat on the arm of the sofa. "This part must be so boring by now." Yuki's shoulders dropped. "So boring." Ada found the old phone video from last spring: Yuki playing a simple minuet, stiff and careful. "Remember when this was hard?" Yuki watched, then laughed. "I sound like a robot." She turned back to the keys and played the bar again.

qa.q: How many evenings in a row had Yuki played the same page?
qa.a: This was the ninth evening in a row.

qa.q: What was Ada feeling as she listened from the kitchen?
qa.a: Ada was worried and unsure how to help, having already tried a reward and an offer to quit that both fell flat.

qa.q: Why did Ada's third approach work better than pizza or quitting?
qa.a: Naming the boredom made Yuki feel understood, and the old video showed real progress that was hard to see day to day.

qa.q: What is it like for Yuki when Ada says the part must be boring?
qa.a: Yuki feels understood and relieved, her shoulders dropping, instead of pressured or doubted.

grounding: Shows a parent moving from rewards and an offer to quit to naming a teen's boredom and pointing to earlier progress on a stuck piece.
